title: Snowdrop
paragraphs: In the middle of winter, when broad snowflakes were drifting down all around, the queen of a country many thousands of miles away sat sewing at her window. The window frame was made of fine black ebony, and as she sat looking out at the snow, she pricked her finger, and three drops of blood fell on the wood. She gazed thoughtfully at the red drops on the white snow and said, “If only my little daughter could be as white as that snow, as red as that blood, and as black as this ebony frame!” And so the little girl did grow up with skin as white as snow, cheeks as rosy as blood, and hair as black as ebony, and she was named Snowdrop.

But this queen died, and before long the king married another wife. She became queen and was very beautiful, but so vain that she could not stand the thought of anyone being lovelier than she was. She owned a magic looking-glass, and she would go to it, gaze at herself, and say:

“Glass, tell me honestly,
Of all the ladies in the land,
Who is the fairest? Tell it to me.”
And the glass had always replied:
“You, my queen, are the fairest in all the land.”

But Snowdrop grew lovelier and lovelier, and by the time she was seven she was radiant as the day and more beautiful than the queen herself. So one day, when the queen went to consult the glass as usual, it replied:

“Fair are you, queen, and fine to see,
But Snowdrop is lovelier far than you!”

When the queen heard this, she turned pale with rage and jealousy. She called one of her servants and said, “Take Snowdrop out into the wide forest, so that I never have to see her again.” The servant led her away, but his heart softened when Snowdrop begged him to spare her life, and he said, “I won’t hurt you, you pretty child.” So he left her alone. He thought it very likely that the wild beasts would tear her to pieces, yet he felt a great weight lift from his heart once he had decided not to kill her but to leave her to her fate, in the hope that someone might find and save her.

Poor Snowdrop wandered through the forest in great fear, and the wild beasts roared around her, but none of them harmed her. In the evening she came to a cottage in the hills and went in to rest, because her little feet could carry her no further. Everything inside was neat and tidy. On the table a white cloth was spread, and there were seven little plates, seven little loaves and seven little glasses of wine, with seven knives and forks set out in order, and along the wall stood seven little beds. She was very hungry, so she nibbled a little from each loaf and drank a few drops from each glass, and then she decided to lie down and rest. She tried all the little beds, but one was too long and another too short, until at last the seventh fitted her, and there she lay down and fell asleep.

Soon afterwards the owners of the cottage came home. They were seven little dwarfs who lived in the mountains and dug and searched for gold. They lit their seven lamps and saw right away that something was wrong. The first said, “Who has been sitting on my stool?” The second said, “Who has been eating from my plate?” The third, “Who has been taking my bread?” The fourth, “Who has been messing with my spoon?” The fifth, “Who has been touching my fork?” The sixth, “Who has been cutting with my knife?” The seventh, “Who has been drinking my wine?” Then the first looked around and said, “Who has been lying in my bed?” The others came running to him, and each one cried out that someone had been in his bed. But the seventh saw Snowdrop and called all his brothers to come and look. They cried out in wonder and amazement, and fetched their lamps to look at her, and said, “Good heavens! What a lovely child she is!” They were delighted to see her and took care not to wake her, and the seventh dwarf slept an hour with each of the others in turn, until the night was over.

In the morning Snowdrop told them her whole story. They felt sorry for her and said that if she would keep everything in order, and cook, wash, knit and spin for them, she could stay where she was and they would take good care of her. Then they went off to work for the whole day, hunting for gold and silver in the mountains, while Snowdrop stayed at home. They warned her, saying, “The queen will soon find out where you are, so be careful and let no one in.”
But the queen, now that she believed Snowdrop was dead, was sure she must be the most beautiful lady in the land. She went to her glass and said:

“Glass, tell me honestly,
Of all the ladies in the land,
Who is the fairest? Tell it to me.”
And the glass replied:

“You, my queen, are the fairest in this land.
But over the hills, in the greenwood shade,
Where the seven dwarfs have made their home,
Snowdrop is hiding her head, and she
Is lovelier far, O queen, than you.”

The queen was terrified, for she knew the glass always told the truth, and she was certain the servant had betrayed her. She could not bear the thought that anyone alive was more beautiful than she was, so she disguised herself as an old pedlar and set off over the hills to the place where the dwarfs lived. She knocked at the door and called, “Fine wares for sale!” Snowdrop looked out of the window and said, “Good day, good woman! What have you got to sell?” “Good wares, fine wares,” said the queen, “laces and cords of every color.” “I can let this old lady in, she seems a perfectly decent person,” thought Snowdrop, and she ran down and unbolted the door. “Goodness me!” said the old woman. “Your bodice is laced so badly! Let me lace it up for you with one of my nice new laces.” Snowdrop suspected no harm, so she stood in front of the old woman. But the woman set to work so quickly and pulled the lace so tight that Snowdrop could not breathe, and she fell down as if dead. “That’s the end of your beauty,” said the spiteful queen, and she went home.

That evening the seven dwarfs came home, and I need hardly say how upset they were to find their faithful Snowdrop stretched out on the floor as if she were quite dead. They lifted her up, and when they saw what was wrong, they cut the lace. After a little while she began to breathe, and soon she came back to life. Then they said, “That old woman was the queen herself. Be careful next time, and let no one in while we are away.”
Back home, the queen hurried to her glass and put the same question to it, and to her bitter distress it gave the same answer:

“You, my queen, are the fairest in this land.
But over the hills, in the greenwood shade,
Where the seven dwarfs have made their home,
Snowdrop is hiding her head, and she
Is lovelier far, O queen, than you.”

Then the blood ran cold in her heart with spite and malice, because Snowdrop was still alive. She disguised herself again, in a quite different outfit from the first, and took a poisoned comb with her. When she reached the dwarfs’ cottage, she knocked at the door and called, “Fine wares for sale!” But Snowdrop said, “I mustn’t let anyone in.” Then the queen said, “Just look at my beautiful combs!” and handed her the poisoned one. It looked so pretty that Snowdrop picked it up and put it in her hair to try it, but the moment it touched her head the poison was so strong that she fell down unconscious. “There you can lie,” said the queen, and she went on her way. But luckily the dwarfs came home very early that evening. When they saw Snowdrop lying on the floor, they guessed what had happened and soon found the poisoned comb. As soon as they took it out she recovered, and she told them everything that had happened, and once more they warned her not to open the door to anyone.

Meanwhile the queen went home to her glass and shook with rage when she heard exactly the same answer as before. She said, “Snowdrop shall die, even if it costs me my own life.” So she went alone into her private room and prepared a poisoned apple. The outside looked rosy and tempting, but anyone who tasted it was sure to die. Then she disguised herself as a peasant’s wife, traveled over the hills to the dwarfs’ cottage and knocked at the door. But Snowdrop put her head out of the window and said, “I mustn’t let anyone in, because the dwarfs have forbidden it.” “As you like,” said the old woman, “but at least take this pretty apple. I’ll give it to you.” “No,” said Snowdrop, “I mustn’t take it.” “Silly girl!” the other replied. “What are you afraid of? Do you think it’s poisoned? Come now, you eat one half and I’ll eat the other.” The apple had been made so that one side was good and only the other side was poisoned. Snowdrop was greatly tempted to taste it, because the apple looked so delicious, and when she saw the old woman take a bite, she could wait no longer. But she had barely put the piece in her mouth when she fell to the ground dead. “This time nothing will save you,” said the queen. She went home to her glass, and at last it said:
“Queen, of all the fair, you are the fairest.”
At that her wicked heart rejoiced, as much as a heart like hers ever could.

When evening came and the dwarfs got home, they found Snowdrop lying on the ground. No breath came from her lips, and they were afraid she was truly dead. They lifted her up, combed her hair and washed her face with wine and water, but it was all in vain: the little girl seemed quite dead. So they laid her on a bier, and all seven sat by her and mourned her for three whole days. Then they thought they should bury her, but her cheeks were still rosy and her face looked just as it had when she was alive, so they said, “We will never bury her in the cold ground.” They made a glass coffin so that they could keep looking at her, and wrote on it in golden letters her name and the fact that she was a king’s daughter. The coffin was placed up in the hills, and one of the dwarfs always sat beside it keeping watch. The birds of the air came too and mourned for Snowdrop, first an owl, then a raven, and finally a dove, and they sat beside her.

And so Snowdrop lay for a long, long time, and she still looked as if she were only sleeping, for even now she was as white as snow, as red as blood and as black as ebony. At last a prince came by and called at the dwarfs’ house. He saw Snowdrop and read what was written in golden letters. He offered the dwarfs money and begged and pleaded with them to let him take her away, but they said, “We won’t give her up for all the gold in the world.” In the end, though, they took pity on him and gave him the coffin. But the moment he lifted it to carry it home, the piece of apple fell from between her lips, and Snowdrop woke up and said, “Where am I?” And the prince said, “You are perfectly safe with me.”

Then he told her everything that had happened. “I love you more than anything in the world,” he said. “Come with me to my father’s palace and be my wife.” Snowdrop agreed and went home with the prince, and the wedding was prepared with great pomp and splendor.
Among the guests invited to the feast was Snowdrop’s old enemy, the queen. While she was putting on her finest clothes, she stood before the glass and said:

“Glass, tell me honestly,
Of all the ladies in the land,
Who is the fairest? Tell it to me.”
And the glass replied:

“You, my lady, are fairest here, I know,
But the new-made queen is fairer still, and so.”

When she heard this, she shook with rage. Yet she was so consumed with envy and curiosity that she could not stay away, and she set out to see the bride. But when she arrived and saw that the bride was none other than Snowdrop, whom she had believed dead for a long time, she choked with fury, fell to the ground and died. Snowdrop and the prince lived and ruled happily over that land for many, many years. Now and then they climbed up into the mountains to visit the little dwarfs, who had been so kind to Snowdrop when she was in need.
